title: P46 (Chester Beatty II): 2 Corinthians 8:4-24 (fols. 68v-69r)
source: P46 (Chester Beatty Biblical Papyrus II, Chester Beatty Library, Dublin): photographs as published in the INTF New Testament Virtual Manuscript Room; Greek from the INTF NTVMR transcription of P46; English from the King James Version
description: 2 Corinthians 8:4-24 in P46, the papyrus codex of Paul's letters copied around 200: fols. 68v-69r, each page with its photograph, the Greek transcription and the King James Version.
introduction:
P46 is a papyrus codex of the letters of Paul copied in Egypt around 200, the oldest surviving collection of Paul's letters. 86 of its 104 leaves survive: 56 in the Chester Beatty Library, Dublin (Biblical Papyrus II, published by Frederic Kenyon in 1934-1937) and 30 in the University of Michigan Library, Ann Arbor (P.Mich. inv. 6238, published by Henry Sanders in 1935). The letters run in the order Romans, Hebrews, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Ephesians, Galatians, Philippians, Colossians and 1 Thessalonians; the first seven leaves (Romans 1:1-5:17) and the end of the book are lost. Hebrews standing after Romans, and the doxology of Romans (16:25-27) standing after 15:33, are among its best-known features.

Each section below is one page side: the holding library's photograph, the NTVMR diplomatic transcription line by line, and the King James Version of every verse that has text on the page. The lower lines of many leaves are lost; the transcribers' restorations are in square brackets.

This entry covers fols. 68v-69r (2 Corinthians 8:4-24).
translator_notes: Greek: the NTVMR diplomatic transcription, line by line as on the papyrus. Square brackets enclose letters that are lost or illegible and were supplied by the transcribers; a dot under a letter marks it as uncertain; [...] marks a gap. Nomina sacra and numerals keep the scribe's overline. Spelling is the scribe's (no accents or breathings). Words broken at a line end stay broken as on the papyrus. Corrections are not shown: the text is the first hand.

English: the King James Version (1611), whole verses, for every verse that has text on the page. A verse that begins on one page and ends on the next is given in full on both. The KJV translates a later form of the Greek text, so its wording does not always match the papyrus; material differences (such as verses the papyrus does not have) are noted in the section.

translation.text: <sup>8:4</sup>Praying us with much intreaty that we would receive the gift, and take upon us the fellowship of the ministering to the saints. <sup>5</sup>And this they did, not as we hoped, but first gave their own selves to the Lord, and unto us by the will of God. <sup>6</sup>Insomuch that we desired Titus, that as he had begun, so he would also finish in you the same grace also. <sup>7</sup>Therefore, as ye abound in every thing, in faith, and utterance, and knowledge, and in all diligence, and in your love to us, see that ye abound in this grace also. <sup>8</sup>I speak not by commandment, but by occasion of the forwardness of others, and to prove the sincerity of your love. <sup>9</sup>For ye know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that, though he was rich, yet for your sakes he became poor, that ye through his poverty might be rich. <sup>10</sup>And herein I give my advice: for this is expedient for you, who have begun before, not only to do, but also to be forward a year ago. <sup>11</sup>Now therefore perform the doing of it; that as there was a readiness to will, so there may be a performance also out of that which ye have. <sup>12</sup>For if there be first a willing mind, it is accepted according to that a man hath, and not according to that he hath not.

translation.text: <sup>8:13</sup>For I mean not that other men be eased, and ye burdened: <sup>14</sup>But by an equality, that now at this time your abundance may be a supply for their want, that their abundance also may be a supply for your want: that there may be equality: <sup>15</sup>As it is written, He that had gathered much had nothing over; and he that had gathered little had no lack. <sup>16</sup>But thanks be to God, which put the same earnest care into the heart of Titus for you. <sup>17</sup>For indeed he accepted the exhortation; but being more forward, of his own accord he went unto you. <sup>18</sup>And we have sent with him the brother, whose praise is in the gospel throughout all the churches; <sup>19</sup>And not that only, but who was also chosen of the churches to travel with us with this grace, which is administered by us to the glory of the same Lord, and declaration of your ready mind: <sup>21</sup>Providing for honest things, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men. <sup>22</sup>And we have sent with them our brother, whom we have oftentimes proved diligent in many things, but now much more diligent, upon the great confidence which I have in you. <sup>23</sup>Whether any do enquire of Titus, he is my partner and fellowhelper concerning you: or our brethren be enquired of, they are the messengers of the churches, and the glory of Christ. <sup>24</sup>Wherefore shew ye to them, and before the churches, the proof of your love, and of our boasting on your behalf.
